hotContext.criticalNews: Post-Q2 delivery beat hangover week: no new production/delivery print. Street consensus for July 22 earnings embeds thin 5.4% op margin and -$3.25B FCF despite 480k deliveries. Full-year volume still only ~1.73M (~5% growth). CA rebate and Latvia/Uruguay entries are incremental demand/footprint positives with limited near-term volume impact.

recentKeyChanges.title: Tesla IR posts Q2 2026 earnings consensus: $27.6B revenue, 1.73M full-year deliveries, -$3.25B FCF
recentKeyChanges.description: Ahead of the July 22 earnings call, Tesla published company-compiled Wall Street consensus from 23 sell-side firms (Barclays, BofA, Goldman, Morgan Stanley, etc.). Street expects Q2 total revenue of $27.58B (auto $20.05B, energy $3.77B, services $3.76B), adjusted non-GAAP EPS $0.55 / GAAP EPS $0.36, gross margin 19.5%, and operating margin only 5.4%. CapEx is pegged at $6.7B with expected free cash flow of -$3.25B for the quarter. Full-year vehicle delivery consensus sits at ~1.73M units — roughly 5–6% growth vs ~1.64M in 2025. That is modest given the Q2 delivery beat (480,126 vs ~406k consensus already reported July 2). H1 deliveries (~838k combining Q1 358,023 + Q2 480,126) imply Tesla needs ~892k H2 deliveries to hit the 1.73M full-year print. Negative FCF and sub-6% operating margin undercut the 'strong auto quarter' narrative: volume beat inventory, not a structural margin or cash-flow re-acceleration.

positive_signals: Q2 delivery beat already printed: 480,126 deliveries vs ~406k consensus (+18%)
Auto revenue expected at $20.05B of $27.58B total
Energy storage contribution expected at $3.77B, supporting diversified revenue
Full-year delivery consensus at 1.73M implies sequential H2 strength needed and assumed by Street
negative_signals: Street expects -$3.25B free cash flow for Q2 despite delivery beat
Operating margin consensus only 5.4% — thin for a supposed volume recovery quarter
Full-year 1.73M deliveries is only ~5–6% YoY growth vs 1.64M in 2025 — not a re-acceleration
Q2 production (451,758) trailed deliveries (480,126) by ~28k — beat was inventory drawdown, not production ramp
Model S/X sunset leaves 'Other' at just 12,364 deliveries / 8,822 produced — Cybertruck still immaterial
CapEx $6.7B expected — heavy spend with negative FCF before Cybercab/Optimus scale

recentKeyChanges.title: Jefferies raises TSLA PT to $400 (from $375) but keeps Hold after Q2 delivery beat
recentKeyChanges.description: Jefferies lifted Tesla's price target to $400 from $375 while maintaining a Hold rating, citing the Q2 automotive delivery surprise (480k vs ~400k Street). Analysts also flagged Robotaxi expansion (Austin→Houston/Dallas/Bay Area/Miami) and SpaceX-merger speculation as catalysts — but warned Optimus and Robotaxi will take years to become meaningful P&L contributors and may carry initial losses. Critical read: a Hold after a >15% delivery beat signals the Street still does not trust sustained auto growth or near-term AI/robot monetization. Delivery strength is being treated as a one-quarter inventory/demand bounce, not a structural re-rating of the car business.

positive_signals: Price target raised $25 to $400 on Q2 delivery outperformance
Q2 deliveries sold through more inventory than produced — demand absorbed available stock
Robotaxi geographic footprint expanding (multi-city) as a longer-term narrative support
negative_signals: Hold rating retained — not an upgrade to Buy despite 15%+ delivery beat
Jefferies flags Optimus/Robotaxi profitability as multi-year and potentially loss-making initially
Merger-speculation risk: TSLA may trade as SpaceX proxy, disconnecting from auto fundamentals
Auto demand case still relies on post-$7,500 federal EV tax credit environment — structural headwind remains

recentKeyChanges.title: California $270M MyFirstEV rebate starts; Model 3/Y qualify but Tesla disadvantaged vs CA-based rivals
recentKeyChanges.description: Gov. Newsom signed SB 168 creating a $270M point-of-sale EV rebate (MyFirstEV), split $135.5M state / $135.5M automaker-funded, to partially replace the expired $7,500 federal EV tax credit. First-time EV buyers get $3,500 off new BEVs with MSRP ≤$50,000; used EVs ≤$25,000 get $1,750. Tesla Model 3 RWD ($42,490), Model 3 LR ($47,490), and base Model Y ($44,990) all qualify. Model S/X/Cybertruck do not. Critical catch: California-based automakers (Rivian, Lucid) are carved out of the $50k price cap entirely — Tesla, headquartered in Texas since 2021, is not. Program goes live later this summer via CARB. Net: modest positive for base 3/Y CA demand, but structural disadvantage vs in-state competitors and only a partial patch for lost federal incentive in Tesla's largest US state market (~1/3 of US EV sales).

positive_signals: Point-of-sale $3,500 rebate on Model 3 and base Model Y improves CA affordability for first-time buyers
California is ~1/3 of US EV sales — any state incentive has non-trivial volume leverage
Replaces some of the demand hole left by expired $7,500 federal EV tax credit
negative_signals: Only $3,500 vs prior $7,500 federal credit — net incentive still much weaker than 2024–2025
Rivian/Lucid exempt from $50k MSRP cap as CA-based makers; Tesla is not — competitive disadvantage
Model S/X/Cybertruck excluded entirely; higher-ASP mix gets zero help
Program not live yet (later this summer); near-term Q3 delivery impact limited until CARB rules finalize
Funded partly by automakers — Tesla will share cost of its own demand subsidy
